stem: A postoperative client reports incisional pain and receives a prescribed analgesic. Which nursing action best demonstrates appropriate evaluation of the intervention?

options.A: Reassess the client's blood pressure and heart rate and use those changes as the primary evidence of pain relief.
options.B: Reassess pain and function when the medication's route and expected onset indicate, and assess for adverse effects.
options.C: Wait until the client requests another analgesic before determining whether the first dose provided adequate relief.
options.D: Observe whether the client is resting quietly and document adequate pain control if no pain behaviors are visible.

rationale: Evaluation after analgesic administration requires reassessing whether the intervention is meeting the client's pain and function goals and assessing for medication effects. The reassessment interval should reflect the medication's route and expected onset rather than an arbitrary delay. When a client can communicate, self-report remains central to pain assessment; physiologic changes and observed behavior may supplement the assessment but should not replace it. Waiting for the client to request another dose does not meet the need for regular evaluation of treatment effectiveness.
educational_objective: After administering an analgesic, reassess pain, function, and relevant adverse effects at a time appropriate to the medication's route and expected onset rather than relying on physiologic signs, visible behavior, or the client's next medication request alone.
source_organization: Open Resources for Nursing (Open RN) / Chippewa Valley Technical College; hosted by NCBI Bookshelf
source_document_title: Nursing Fundamentals [Internet], 2nd edition, Part XI: Comfort
source_locator: Part XI Comfort > 11.5 Applying the Nursing Process > Assessment: pain is subjective and client self-report is central when the client can communicate; Evaluation: regularly evaluate whether interventions meet pain-management and function goals, and after analgesics reassess at a time frame based on route, onset, and peak. See also 11.4 Pain Management/11.5 Planning Interventions for monitoring and management of analgesic adverse effects.
source_claim_supported: After an analgesic, the nurse should reassess pain and function at a time appropriate to the medication route and expected effect, while evaluating medication effects; self-report remains central when the client can communicate.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Appendix A, Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, p. 38: Evaluate client response to medication; Administer medications for pain management; assess client for actual and potential side effects and adverse effects of medications.
blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — evaluation of analgesic response
correction_summary: Rebuilt all four options to remove the absolute-word distractor cue and the long keyed-answer pattern, preserved the analgesic-evaluation construct, tightened the source locator, and remapped the primary NCLEX client need to the more direct Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies activity statement for evaluating medication response.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Postoperative pain management — evaluation after analgesic administration
audit_findings.stem: PASS — concise postoperative context with a communicative client and a clear evaluation task.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS as distractor — vital signs can contribute objective data but are not the primary measure of pain relief when the client can self-report.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS — directly reflects ongoing evaluation of pain/function, route/onset-appropriate timing, and medication effects; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — waiting for another request omits the required regular reassessment of treatment effectiveness.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — quiet rest or absence of visible pain behavior does not substitute for reassessment of a communicative client's pain and function.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — B is the only option that performs active, source-supported post-analgesic evaluation.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — A and D use incomplete proxy measures; C improperly defers evaluation.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — option lengths are tightly matched and no keyed-option-only absolute-word pattern remains.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — the 2026 NCSBN Test Plan directly lists evaluation of client response to medication and administration of medications for pain management under Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether physiologic signs, visible comfort, or client-initiated PRN requests could independently establish analgesic effectiveness; none provides the complete evaluation required by the source, leaving B as the single best answer.
